changes: In lesson01, you learned how dominant and recessive alleles can relate to an organism's appearance. Mendel had to discover that relationship from evidence. He chose plants with contrasting characteristics, controlled which plants reproduced, and followed their offspring. We will reconstruct that experiment first. Then we will use what we know about chromosomes to explain the pattern he found.

Gregor Mendel helped establish the ideas of dominant and recessive inheritance by studying pea plants. He wanted to understand how characteristics passed from parents to offspring. Would crossing plants with contrasting traits produce a blend, or would the offspring show one form rather than the other? To follow his investigation, start with the plants he chose and then examine what happened in each generation.
As you learned in lesson01, a dominant phenotype alone can leave more than one genotype possible.
A plant with the dominant phenotype can carry two copies of the dominant allele or one dominant and one recessive allele. Appearance alone cannot distinguish those combinations.
Lesson03 will make the grid and probability operations systematic. Lesson05 will ask how following a second gene changes the gamete problem.

Next, we will use single-trait crosses to practise setting up grids and calculating probabilities. When we turn to two-trait crosses, we will ask how following a second gene changes the gamete problem.
